sections.title: Gradient Descent Revisited — Slow Plateaus and Contour Maps

blocks.html: Start here Week 2 gave us gradient descent. This week asks: is it fast? The answer: not always. On flat regions of the error surface it crawls. Before we fix that with better optimisers, we learn a simple tool to see what an optimiser is doing — the contour map.
blocks.text:
Start here Week 2 gave us gradient descent. This
week asks: is it fast? The answer: not always. On flat
regions of the error surface it crawls. Before we fix that with better
optimisers, we learn a simple tool to see what an optimiser is
doing — the contour map .
1. Quick recap (from Week 2)

blocks.html:
• Sigmoid neuron f(x) = 1/(1 + e^(−(wx + b))), data (0.5, 0.2) and (2.5, 0.9).
  • Loss L(w, b) = (1/N) Σ (yᵢ − f(xᵢ))². Guessing (w, b) by hand works for 2 parameters but not for millions.
  • From the Taylor series: the loss falls fastest when we move opposite to the gradient.
  • Update rule: w_{t+1} = w_t − η∇w_t, b_{t+1} = b_t − η∇b_t.
  • For the sigmoid neuron: ∇w = Σ (f(xᵢ) − yᵢ) f(xᵢ)(1 − f(xᵢ)) xᵢ, ∇b = Σ (f(xᵢ) − yᵢ) f(xᵢ)(1 − f(xᵢ)).
blocks.text:

2. Steep slopes and gentle
slopes

blocks.html: The gradient is the slope Δy/Δx of the loss curve.
blocks.text:
The gradient is the slope Δy/Δx of the loss
curve.

blocks.html:
• Where the curve is steep, the gradient is large.
  • Where the curve is gentle, the gradient is small.
blocks.text: Where the curve is steep , the gradient is large . Where the curve is gentle , the gradient is small .

blocks.html: Our update is η∇w. So:
blocks.text: Our update is η∇w. So:

blocks.html:
• On steep parts → big steps.
  • On gentle parts → tiny steps.
blocks.text: On steep parts → big steps. On gentle parts → tiny steps.

blocks.alt: A ball on a curve takes big steps on the steep part and tiny steps on the flat part
blocks.caption:
Step size follows the slope: fast on steep ground, very slow on flat
ground.

blocks.html: Lecture example — starting points Run gradient descent for t_max = 150 steps from (w, b) = (−2, 2), and again from (−3, 2). Whatever the starting point, once the path reaches a gentle region, progress slows down a lot. Starting from (−4, −4) is even worse — the loss there is almost flat.
blocks.text:

blocks.html: Everyday example Rolling a marble on a nearly flat table: it barely moves, even though the floor (the minimum) is somewhere ahead.
blocks.text:
Everyday example Rolling a marble on a nearly flat
table: it barely moves, even though the floor (the minimum) is somewhere

3. Contours: seeing
the surface from the top

blocks.html: 3D plots are hard to read. A contour map is a 2D way to show the same surface.
blocks.text:
3D plots are hard to read. A contour map is a 2D way
to show the same surface.

blocks.html: How it’s made: take horizontal slices of the error surface at equal heights (equal loss values). Look from the top. Each slice becomes a closed line — a contour. Every point on one contour has the same loss.
blocks.text:
How it’s made: take horizontal slices of the error
surface at equal heights (equal loss values). Look from the top. Each
slice becomes a closed line — a contour . Every point on
one contour has the same loss .

blocks.alt: A 3D loss hill is sliced at equal heights and seen from above as a map of contour lines
blocks.caption: Lines close together = steep; lines far apart = gentle.

blocks.html: How to read a contour map:
blocks.text: How to read a contour map:

blocks.html:
What you see What it means
Contours close together steep slope in that direction
Contours far apart gentle slope
Innermost small ring the minimum (lowest loss)
blocks.text: What you see What it means Contours close together steep slope in that direction Contours far apart gentle slope Innermost small ring the minimum (lowest loss)

blocks.html: This is exactly like height lines on a trekking map of a hill.
blocks.text: This is exactly like height lines on a trekking map of a hill.

blocks.html: Gradient descent on a contour map: the path always crosses contours at right angles (the gradient is perpendicular to the contour line). Where contours are far apart, the dots of the path bunch together — tiny steps.
blocks.text:

together — tiny steps.
4. The problem to solve

blocks.html: Plain gradient descent:
blocks.text: Plain gradient descent:

blocks.html:
• takes a lot of time to cross regions with a gentle slope,
  • because the gradient there is very small.
blocks.text: takes a lot of time to cross regions with a gentle slope , because the gradient there is very small .

blocks.html: Can we do better? Yes — momentum-based gradient descent (next page).
blocks.text:
Can we do better? Yes — momentum-based gradient
descent (next page).

blocks.html: One more thing to keep in mind: every optimiser starts by computing ∇w₀ at the starting point.
blocks.text: One more thing to keep in mind: every optimiser starts by computing ∇w₀ at the starting point.

blocks.html: In one line: Gradient descent moves fast on steep slopes and crawls on gentle ones; contour maps show the error surface from the top, where close lines mean steep and far lines mean gentle.

Quick check

blocks.html:
1. On a contour map, two neighbouring lines are very close in the w-direction. What does that tell you?
The loss changes quickly in the w-direction — the slope along w is steep.
blocks.text:
On a contour map, two neighbouring lines are very close in the
w-direction. What does that tell you? The loss changes quickly in the w-direction — the slope along w is
steep.

blocks.html:
1. Why does gradient descent slow down on a plateau?
The step is η × gradient, and on a plateau the gradient is close to 0, so the steps are tiny.
blocks.text:
Why does gradient descent slow down on a plateau? The step is η × gradient, and on a plateau the gradient is close to 0,
so the steps are tiny.

blocks.html:
1. All points on one contour line have the same ___.
Loss (error) value.

blocks.html:
1. ∇w = 0.001, η = 1. How far does w move in one step?
0.001 — a very small step.

sections.title: Momentum-Based Gradient Descent and Nesterov Accelerated Gradient

blocks.html: Start here If someone keeps telling you “go left… go left… go left”, you start walking faster to the left. Momentum does exactly this: it remembers past gradients and builds up speed. It crosses flat regions quickly — but it can overshoot. Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) fixes the overshooting by looking ahead before stepping.
blocks.text:
Start here If someone keeps telling you “go left… go
left… go left”, you start walking faster to the left. Momentum does exactly this: it remembers past gradients
and builds up speed. It crosses flat regions quickly — but it can
overshoot. Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) fixes
the overshooting by looking ahead before stepping.
1. Momentum: the intuition

blocks.html: If I am repeatedly asked to move in the same direction, I should gain confidence and take bigger steps in that direction — just like a ball rolling down a slope gains momentum.
blocks.text:
If I am repeatedly asked to move in the same
direction , I should gain confidence and take bigger
steps in that direction — just like a ball rolling down a slope
gains momentum.

blocks.alt: A ball rolling down a slope speeds up, overshoots the valley, and swings back
blocks.caption:
Momentum = remember the past direction; speed builds up, but it may
overshoot.

blocks.text: 2. The update rule

blocks.html: u_t = β u_{t−1} + ∇w_t w_{t+1} = w_t − η u_t
blocks.text:
u_t = β u_{t−1} + ∇w_t w_{t+1} = w_t − η
u_t

blocks.html: with u₋₁ = 0, w₀ random, and 0 ≤ β < 1 (β is the momentum factor, often 0.9).
blocks.text:
with u₋₁ = 0, w₀ random, and 0 ≤ β < 1 (β is the
momentum factor, often 0.9).

blocks.html: So besides the current gradient, we also look at the history of updates.
blocks.text:
So besides the current gradient, we also look at the history
of updates .

3. Unrolling: an
exponentially weighted average

blocks.html:
• u₀ = β·0 + ∇w₀ = ∇w₀
  • u₁ = βu₀ + ∇w₁ = β∇w₀ + ∇w₁
  • u₂ = βu₁ + ∇w₂ = β(β∇w₀ + ∇w₁) + ∇w₂ = β²∇w₀ + β∇w₁ + ∇w₂
  • In general: u_t = Σ_τ₌₀ᵗ β^(t−τ) ∇w_τ
blocks.text: u₀ = β·0 + ∇w₀ = ∇w₀ u₁ = βu₀ + ∇w₁ = β∇w₀ + ∇w₁ u₂ = βu₁ + ∇w₂ = β(β∇w₀ + ∇w₁) + ∇w₂ = β²∇w₀ + β∇w₁ + ∇w₂ In general: u_t = Σ_τ₌₀ᵗ β^(t−τ) ∇w_τ

blocks.html: u_t is an exponentially weighted sum of the current and all past gradients. Recent gradients get weight close to 1; old ones fade (β, β², β³, …).
blocks.text:
u_t is an exponentially weighted sum of the current and all
past gradients . Recent gradients get weight close to 1; old
ones fade (β, β², β³, …).

blocks.html: Feel it: if the gradient is always 1 and β = 0.9:
blocks.text:
Feel it: if the gradient is always 1 and β =
0.9:

blocks.html:
t u_t = 0.9 u_{t−1} + 1
0 1
1 0.9 × 1 + 1 = 1.9
2 0.9 × 1.9 + 1 = 2.71
3 0.9 × 2.71 + 1 = 3.439
… grows towards 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10
So on a long gentle slope, momentum can take steps up to 10 times bigger than plain gradient descent.
blocks.text:
So on a long gentle slope, momentum can take steps up to 10
times bigger than plain gradient descent.
4. The code (and a small fix)

blocks.html:
def do_mgd(max_epochs):
    w, b, eta = -2, -2, 1.0
    prev_uw, prev_ub, beta = 0, 0, 0.9
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        dw, db = 0, 0
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):
            dw += grad_w(w, b, x, y)
            db += grad_b(w, b, x, y)
        uw = beta * prev_uw + eta * dw
        ub = beta * prev_ub + eta * db
        w = w - uw          # the slide writes "w - vw" — a typo; it must be uw
        b = b - ub          # likewise "b - vb" should be ub
        prev_uw = uw
        prev_ub = ub
blocks.text: def do_mgd(max_epochs): w, b, eta = - 2 , - 2 , 1.0 prev_uw, prev_ub, beta = 0 , 0 , 0.9 for i in range (max_epochs): dw, db = 0 , 0 for x, y in zip (X, Y): dw += grad_w(w, b, x, y) db += grad_b(w, b, x, y) uw = beta * prev_uw + eta * dw ub = beta * prev_ub + eta * db w = w - uw # the slide writes "w - vw" — a typo; it must be uw b = b - ub # likewise "b - vb" should be ub prev_uw = uw prev_ub = ub

blocks.html: Note: the code puts η inside u (u = βu + η∇w, then w = w − u). The formula above puts η outside (w = w − ηu). With a fixed η these are the same thing — the code’s u is just η times the formula’s u.
blocks.text:
Note: the code puts η inside u (u = βu + η∇w, then w
= w − u). The formula above puts η outside (w = w − ηu). With a fixed η
these are the same thing — the code’s u is just η times the formula’s
u.
5. Is moving fast always good?

blocks.html: Good: even on gentle slopes, momentum takes large steps because the built-up momentum carries it along.
blocks.text:
Good: even on gentle slopes, momentum takes large steps because the built-up momentum carries it
along.

blocks.html: Bad: it can overshoot the goal. In a narrow valley (error high on both sides of the minimum), momentum oscillates in and out of the valley and takes many U-turns before settling.
blocks.text:
Bad: it can overshoot the goal. In
a narrow valley (error high on both sides of the minimum), momentum oscillates in and out of the valley and takes many U-turns before settling.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the race Start w₀ = −2, b₀ = −4, η = 1, on a surface with a narrow valley. After 50 iterations, momentum has reached an error of 0.00001, while plain gradient descent is still stuck at 0.16. So, despite the U-turns, momentum still converges much faster than plain gradient descent.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the race Start w₀ = −2, b₀ = −4, η
= 1, on a surface with a narrow valley. After 50 iterations, momentum
has reached an error of 0.00001 , while plain gradient
descent is still stuck at 0.16 . So, despite the
U-turns, momentum still converges much faster than
plain gradient descent.

6.
Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG): look before you leap

blocks.html: Can we reduce the oscillations? Yes.
blocks.text: Can we reduce the oscillations? Yes.

blocks.html: From u_t = βu_{t−1} + ∇w_t we know we are going to move at least by βu_{t−1}, and then a bit more by the gradient. So why not first jump to where momentum will take us, measure the gradient there, and then decide?
blocks.text:
From u_t = βu_{t−1} + ∇w_t we know we are going to move at
least by βu_{t−1}, and then a bit more by the gradient. So why
not first jump to where momentum will take us , measure
the gradient there , and then decide?

blocks.html: NAG update:
blocks.text: NAG update:

blocks.html: u_t = β u_{t−1} + ∇(w_t − β u_{t−1}) w_{t+1} = w_t − η u_t

(In the lecture’s code form, where η is inside u, the look-ahead point is w − β·prev_v; in the formula form above, it is w_t − ηβu_{t−1}. Same idea: step to where momentum is taking you, then measure.)
blocks.text:
(In the lecture’s code form, where η is inside u, the look-ahead
point is w − β·prev_v; in the formula form above, it is w_t − ηβu_{t−1}.
Same idea: step to where momentum is taking you, then measure.)

blocks.alt: NAG takes the momentum step first, measures the gradient at the look-ahead point, then corrects; momentum measures at the current point
blocks.caption:
Momentum measures the slope where it stands; NAG measures it where
it is about to land.

blocks.html:
def do_nag(max_epochs):
    w, b, eta = -2, -2, 1.0
    prev_vw, prev_vb, beta = 0, 0, 0.9
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        dw, db = 0, 0
        # partial update: where momentum alone would take us
        v_w = beta * prev_vw
        v_b = beta * prev_vb
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):
            # look ahead: gradient at the look-ahead point
            dw += grad_w(w - v_w, b - v_b, x, y)
            db += grad_b(w - v_w, b - v_b, x, y)
        vw = beta * prev_vw + eta * dw
        vb = beta * prev_vb + eta * db
        w = w - vw
        b = b - vb
        prev_vw = vw
        prev_vb = vb
blocks.text: def do_nag(max_epochs): w, b, eta = - 2 , - 2 , 1.0 prev_vw, prev_vb, beta = 0 , 0 , 0.9 for i in range (max_epochs): dw, db = 0 , 0 # partial update: where momentum alone would take us v_w = beta * prev_vw v_b = beta * prev_vb for x, y in zip (X, Y): # look ahead: gradient at the look-ahead point dw += grad_w(w - v_w, b - v_b, x, y) db += grad_b(w - v_w, b - v_b, x, y) vw = beta * prev_vw + eta * dw vb = beta * prev_vb + eta * db w = w - vw b = b - vb prev_vw = vw prev_vb = vb

blocks.html: Why it helps: if momentum is about to overshoot, the gradient at the look-ahead point already points back, so NAG corrects its course earlier. Its oscillations are smaller, and it is less likely to escape the minimum valley.
blocks.text:
Why it helps: if momentum is about to overshoot, the
gradient at the look-ahead point already points back ,
so NAG corrects its course earlier . Its oscillations
are smaller , and it is less likely to escape the
minimum valley.
7. Comparing the three

blocks.alt: Three paths on the same contour map: plain GD barely moves, momentum overshoots with big U-turns, NAG makes smaller U-turns
blocks.caption:
Same start, same η: GD crawls, momentum overshoots, NAG overshoots
less.

blocks.html:
Method Uses Strength Weakness
Gradient descent current gradient only stable very slow on gentle slopes
Momentum current + past gradients fast on gentle slopes overshoots, many U-turns
NAG gradient at the look-ahead point + past fast, shorter U-turns slightly more bookkeeping
blocks.text: Method Uses Strength Weakness Gradient descent current gradient only stable very slow on gentle slopes Momentum current + past gradients fast on gentle slopes overshoots, many U-turns NAG gradient at the look-ahead point + past fast, shorter U-turns slightly more bookkeeping

Quick check

blocks.html:
1. β = 0.5, gradients ∇w₀ = 2, ∇w₁ = 2, ∇w₂ = 2. Find u₂.
u₀ = 2; u₁ = 0.5×2 + 2 = 3; u₂ = 0.5×3 + 2 = 3.5.

1. What is the weight of ∇w₀ inside u₃ when β = 0.9?
β³ = 0.729.
blocks.text: What is the weight of ∇w₀ inside u₃ when β = 0.9? β³ = 0.729.

blocks.html:
1. What happens with β = 0?
u_t = ∇w_t, so momentum becomes plain gradient descent.
blocks.text: What happens with β = 0? u_t = ∇w_t, so momentum becomes plain gradient descent.

blocks.html:
1. Where does NAG compute the gradient?
At the look-ahead point — where the momentum step alone would take the parameters — not at the current point.
blocks.text:
Where does NAG compute the gradient? At the look-ahead point — where the momentum step alone would take the
parameters — not at the current point.

blocks.html:
1. Why can momentum leave the minimum valley?
Its accumulated velocity carries it past the minimum and up the other side before the gradient can slow it down.
blocks.text:
Why can momentum leave the minimum valley? Its accumulated velocity carries it past the minimum and up the other
side before the gradient can slow it down.

blocks.html: Start here With a million training examples, plain gradient descent does a million calculations just to take one step. That is very slow. Stochastic gradient descent updates after every single example; mini-batch gradient descent updates after a small group. This page explains the trade-off: speed versus noisy steps.
blocks.text:
Start here With a million training examples, plain
gradient descent does a million calculations just to take one step. That is very slow. Stochastic gradient descent updates after every
single example; mini-batch gradient descent
updates after a small group. This page explains the trade-off: speed
versus noisy steps.

1. Batch (vanilla) gradient
descent

blocks.html:
def do_gradient_descent():
    w, b, eta, max_epochs = -2, -2, 1.0, 1000
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        dw, db = 0, 0
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):          # go over ALL the data
            dw += grad_w(x, w, b, y)
            db += grad_b(x, w, b, y)
        w = w - eta * dw                 # then update ONCE
        b = b - eta * db
blocks.text: def do_gradient_descent(): w, b, eta, max_epochs = - 2 , - 2 , 1.0 , 1000 for i in range (max_epochs): dw, db = 0 , 0 for x, y in zip (X, Y): # go over ALL the data dw += grad_w(x, w, b, y) db += grad_b(x, w, b, y) w = w - eta * dw # then update ONCE b = b - eta * db

blocks.html: The algorithm goes over the entire data once before updating the parameters.
blocks.text:
The algorithm goes over the entire data once before
updating the parameters.

blocks.html: Why? Because this sum is the true gradient of the loss (the loss is the sum of the losses of all points). No approximation. So the theory holds: each step is guaranteed to decrease the loss (for a small enough η).
blocks.text:
Why? Because this sum is the true
gradient of the loss (the loss is the sum of the losses of all
points). No approximation. So the theory holds: each step is
guaranteed to decrease the loss (for a small enough η).

blocks.html: The flip side: with a million points, one update needs a million gradient calculations. Very slow.
blocks.text:
The flip side: with a million points, one update needs a million gradient
calculations. Very slow.

2. Stochastic gradient descent
(SGD)

blocks.html:
def do_stochastic_gradient_descent():
    w, b, eta, max_epochs = -2, -2, 1.0, 1000
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):
            dw = grad_w(x, w, b, y)      # gradient of ONE point
            db = grad_b(x, w, b, y)
            w = w - eta * dw             # update immediately
            b = b - eta * db
blocks.text: def do_stochastic_gradient_descent(): w, b, eta, max_epochs = - 2 , - 2 , 1.0 , 1000 for i in range (max_epochs): for x, y in zip (X, Y): dw = grad_w(x, w, b, y) # gradient of ONE point db = grad_b(x, w, b, y) w = w - eta * dw # update immediately b = b - eta * db

blocks.html: The algorithm updates the parameters for every single data point. With a million points, that is a million updates per pass.
blocks.text:
The algorithm updates the parameters for every single data
point . With a million points, that is a million updates per
pass.

blocks.html: Two words to know:
blocks.text: Two words to know:

blocks.html:
• 1 epoch = one pass over the entire data
  • 1 step = one update of the parameters
blocks.text: 1 epoch = one pass over the entire data 1 step = one update of the parameters

blocks.html: The flip side: it is an approximate (stochastic = random-ish) gradient. We estimate the total gradient from one data point — almost like tossing a coin once and estimating P(heads). There is no guarantee that each step decreases the loss.
blocks.text:
The flip side: it is an approximate (stochastic = random-ish) gradient. We estimate the total gradient from one data point — almost like tossing a coin once and estimating P(heads). There is no
guarantee that each step decreases the loss.
3. Why SGD oscillates

blocks.html: SGD makes greedy decisions. Each point pushes the parameters in the direction best for itself, without knowing how this affects the other points. An update that is good for one point may hurt others — it’s almost as if the data points are competing with each other. Result: many oscillations.
blocks.text:
SGD makes greedy decisions. Each point pushes the
parameters in the direction best for itself , without
knowing how this affects the other points. An update that is good for
one point may hurt others — it’s almost as if the data
points are competing with each other. Result: many oscillations .

blocks.html: Everyday example A class decides where to go for a trip. If the teacher changes the plan after each single student’s opinion, the plan keeps flip-flopping. If she asks a group of 25 students each time, the plan changes more steadily.
blocks.text:
Everyday example A class decides where to go for a
trip. If the teacher changes the plan after each single student’s
opinion, the plan keeps flip-flopping. If she asks a group of 25
students each time, the plan changes more steadily.
4. Mini-batch gradient descent

blocks.html: Improve the estimate: update after seeing B points (a mini-batch), not 1.
blocks.text:
Improve the estimate: update after seeing B points
(a mini-batch ), not 1.

blocks.html:
def do_minibatch_stochastic_gradient_descent():
    w, b, eta, max_epochs = -2, -2, 1.0, 500
    mini_batch_size = 25
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        dw, db, num_points_seen = 0, 0, 0
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):
            dw += grad_w(x, w, b, y)
            db += grad_b(x, w, b, y)
            num_points_seen += 1
            if num_points_seen % mini_batch_size == 0:
                w = w - eta * dw         # update after every 25 points
                b = b - eta * db
                dw, db = 0, 0            # reset for the next batch

sections.title: Choosing the Learning Rate and Momentum, and Line Search

blocks.html: Start here The learning rate η decides how big every step is. Too small and training crawls; too big and it jumps around wildly. This page gives practical tips to pick η, ways to shrink it over time (annealing), a schedule for momentum, and line search — trying several η at every step.
blocks.text:
Start here The learning rate η decides how big every
step is. Too small and training crawls; too big and it jumps around
wildly. This page gives practical tips to pick η, ways to shrink
it over time (annealing), a schedule for momentum, and line search — trying several η at every step.

1. Why not just use a big
learning rate?

blocks.html: Idea: gentle slopes give tiny gradients, so multiply them by a large η to make the steps bigger.
blocks.text: Idea: gentle slopes give tiny gradients, so multiply them by a large η to make the steps bigger.

blocks.html: Lecture example — η = 10 On gentle regions this helps. But on steep regions, the already large gradient is blown up even more. The parameters jump far past the minimum and the loss jumps around.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — η = 10 On gentle regions this
helps. But on steep regions, the already large gradient
is blown up even more. The parameters jump far past the minimum and the
loss jumps around.

blocks.html: What we’d like is a learning rate that adjusts itself to the gradient — big where the slope is gentle, small where it is steep. Such adaptive algorithms come next in the course (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam).
blocks.text:
What we’d like is a learning rate that adjusts itself to the
gradient — big where the slope is gentle, small where it is

blocks.text:
2. Tips for the initial
learning rate

blocks.html:
1. Tune on a log scale: try 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0.
  2. Run a few epochs with each; find the one that works best.
  3. Do a finer search around it. If 0.1 was best, now try 0.05, 0.2, 0.3.

3. Tips for
annealing (decaying) the learning rate

blocks.html: Start with a reasonable η and reduce it as training goes on.

5. Line search

blocks.html: In practice a line search is often done to find a better η at each step.
blocks.text:
In practice a line search is often done to find a
better η at each step.

blocks.html:
def do_line_search_gradient_descent(max_epochs):
    w, b, etas = -2, -2, [0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 10]
    for i in range(max_epochs):
        dw, db = 0, 0
        for x, y in zip(X, Y):
            dw += grad_w(w, b, x, y)
            db += grad_b(w, b, x, y)
        min_error = 10000                    # some large value
        for eta in etas:                     # try every candidate
            temp_w = w - eta * dw
            temp_b = b - eta * db
            if error(temp_w, temp_b) < min_error:
                best_w, best_b = temp_w, temp_b
                min_error = error(best_w, best_b)
        w, b = best_w, best_b                # keep the best one

Compute the gradient once, try every η, keep the step with the
lowest loss.

  • Keep the updated value that gives the lowest loss.
  • So at each step we use the best η from the available choices.

The story in 6 lines

blocks.html:
1. Gradient descent steps are η × slope → tiny steps on gentle slopes.
  2. Contour maps: lines close together = steep, far apart = gentle.
  3. Momentum: remember past gradients (u_t = βu_{t−1} + ∇w_t) → fast on flat regions, but overshoots with U-turns.
  4. NAG: measure the gradient at the look-ahead point → shorter U-turns.
  5. SGD / mini-batch: update after 1 / B points → many more updates per epoch, but noisy.
  6. Learning rate: search on a log scale, decay over time, or pick per step with line search.

Key formulas

blocks.html:
Method Update
Gradient descent w_{t+1} = w_t − η∇w_t
Momentum u_t = βu_{t−1} + ∇w_t; w_{t+1} = w_t − ηu_t (u₋₁ = 0, 0 ≤ β < 1)
Momentum unrolled u_t = Σ_τ₌₀ᵗ β^(t−τ) ∇w_τ
NAG u_t = βu_{t−1} + ∇(w_t − βu_{t−1}); w_{t+1} = w_t − ηu_t
Exponential decay η = η₀ e^(−kt)
1/t decay η = η₀ / (1 + kt)
Step decay halve η every few epochs, or when validation error rises
Sutskever momentum β_t = min(1 − 2^(−1 − log₂(⌊t/250⌋ + 1)), β_max)

Common traps

blocks.html:
• In the code, η is inside u (u = βu + η∇w, w = w − u); in the formula it is outside. Same result for a fixed η.
  • The momentum code on the slide writes “w = w − vw” — it should be uw (typo).
  • The exponential decay slide prints “η₀^(−kt)”; the standard formula is η₀e^(−kt).
  • β = 0 turns momentum back into plain gradient descent.
  • A larger batch reduces, but never fully removes, the oscillations (unless B = N).
  • The lecture’s title also lists AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam, but these slides end at line search — the adaptive methods are in the next set of lectures.

1. What problem does NAG fix in momentum?
The large overshoots/oscillations — by computing the gradient at the look-ahead point it corrects course earlier.
